article.title: The Health Insurance Experience
article.author: Rochester Red Star: News from Rochester DSA
article.content: by Sara C The following text is adapted from a speech delivered by Sara C at the NY Health Act Rally held October 17 at Rochester’s Liberty Pole. Despite health insurance being the primary way most Americans access any kind of health care, it’s not exactly popular. It can be expensive, not just in the premiums we pay for it with every paycheck, but also with deductibles that mean coverage doesn’t even start until you’ve paid a certain amount out of pocket. The coverage itself can be frustratingly limited. Beyond all that, health insurance companies have plenty of tactics to avoid payment and accountability. This is my story of fighting against health insurance companies’ duplicitous practices, what I’ve learned from it, and what I see as a potential (if partial) solution. I was diagnosed with Type 1 diabetes when I was 8 years old. I will need insulin injections or infusions for the rest of my life to stay alive, because my body is incapable of making its own. There is no cure for type 1 diabetes at this point in time, and there is no way to treat it without insulin. Like many chronic illnesses, treatment plans vary from person to person. Some diabetics do better on injections and some do better on insulin pumps. Among pump users, different pumps address different needs that people have. Endocrinologists generally agree that finding the right system for the individual increases length and quality of life, which is generally the goal of medicine! In 2024, I started ordering pump supplies through a supply distribution company and billing it to my employer-funded insurance, who allegedly told the distributor that I was covered. Months later, I started getting bills for the full price of my pump supplies. I then spent two (2) years on the phone at least once a week with insurance and supply companies, submitting appeals and detailed information including letters from my doctor, only for the final result to be that they still refused to cover my pump supplies because they’re a “plan exception”. There was only one pump they covered, and it was one I had tried but hadn’t had success with. I’m lucky that I have generous friends and family who contributed to helping me pay out of pocket this past year, which came to about $2,000. That’s nothing to an insurance company. It’s unaffordable for me. I was so stressed about this that I started having chest pains. I had some tests done to make sure it was nothing more serious than anxiety and stress. (It wasn’t.) Unfortunately, I have a 10% co-insurance for such tests, and it turns out they’re very expensive, so I also owed over $500 for those. While I was dealing with this, I found out that the mammogram I got this February – because I have a family history of breast cancer – was also not covered because I was not yet 40. No exceptions for family history, and no exceptions for being only a few months short of 40. That was another $300 added to my medical payments and debt. I also pay about $50 a month in co-pays for my insulin, my continuous glucose monitor (CGM), and other medications. If that weren’t enough, I’m now getting immunotherapy injections so I can go outdoors in the summer without my eyes becoming unbearably itchy, which costs me $50 per week, a co-pay that is only $5 less than the full charge. I now have my pump supplies covered because I emailed my HR department, desperate, and gave them the intimate details of my medical needs. They had my pump and its supplies specifically added to the plan, two years after I had been fighting with the insurance company and all they had told me was no. Not one insurance rep suggested that I ask my company to add it to the plan. I shouldn’t have had to do any of that to get my medical needs met. The only reason health insurance companies exist is to generate profit by denying people care. That’s literally it. I suspect that “plan exceptions” will become more popular with insurance companies in the coming years, as a tactic to deny care and increase profits. I have also noticed that communication between patient and health insurance has become more and more opaque. When I asked for a list of “plan exceptions”, I was told that was not possible. Whether it didn’t exist, or the person I spoke to just didn’t have access to it, I don’t know. That’s another tactic: they set call center employees up with a script, don’t give them any more information than they give the patient, and limit their ability to escalate. They also don’t save notes about your case in a way that makes it easy for successive call center employees to access, so you have to fully explain why you’re calling every single time before you run into the brick wall of their inability to do anything about it. This makes calling to try and get something covered an enraging and Sisyphean task, and many people just give up and pay out of pocket. Many plans, like mine, also have medical and pharmacy coverage separated under different companies who don’t communicate with each other. While trying to get coverage for my pump supplies, my medical insurance told me it wasn’t covered by them as durable medical equipment (DME), so it should be covered under pharmacy, but when I called the pharmacy insurance, they said the opposite, sending me in circles with no accountability. This is not poor system design. This is how the system was fully intended to be designed so that executives and shareholders make as much money as possible. Private health insurance kills people in a myriad of ways: A lack of health insurance kills people. We’ve all heard the stories of diabetics like me who die because they lost insurance and can’t afford insulin. (I won’t go into details about how diabetic ketoacidosis is a horrible way to die, but trust me, it is.) Even people who do have health insurance die because their condition or its treatment isn’t covered and they can’t afford it. There are also the people who die by suicide rather than continue to fight tooth and nail just to survive every day. All of this is about to increase because of federal cuts. Scientists at UPenn predicted last year that Trump’s cuts could lead to 51,000 preventable deaths per year. Then, there are the people who survive but can’t thrive, because they can only access limited or less appropriate treatments. Or they are forced into poverty to pay for care. Doctors know that stress can have a severely negative impact on your health, so it’s hard to actually get healthy when you’re constantly fighting with insurance, or aren’t sure where your next meal or rent check is coming from. //Health insurance functions as a tool to keep working class people oppressed. One in four employed people in the U.S. stay at their job because they don’t want to lose health insurance, even though they would like to leave. Employers absolutely use this as a threat to keep workers in line. If you search on social media, you will see thousands of stories like mine, and even doctors advocating for their patients who were denied insurance coverage. It is abundantly clear that my insurance story is not a one-off, and not even particularly horrific, relatively speaking: I came through with no long-term negative health effects, no brushes with starvation or homelessness. Many Americans are not so lucky. So, what can we do? A great first step is to get the New York Health Act (NYHA) passed. This is a bill that has been floating in the state legislature for 35 years, and it would create a universal single-payer health care system in New York. It would be funded by a progressive income tax that is far, far lower than most of us are paying right now in premiums alone. Such a tax would have the wealthy paying their fair share to keep everyone in the state healthy. There would be no premiums, no co-payments, no co-insurance, no deductibles: all New York residents get full coverage and pay only the tax. It would eliminate the need for private health insurance: even health care while traveling interstate would be covered. (For more information, please see nyhcampaign.org .) Of course, there are many other problems in our healthcare system: for-profit hospitals and medical centers, leading to staff shortages; a for-profit pharmaceutical industry; medical racism, misogyny, fatphobia, and lots of other biases that affect care; and the fact that the lack of universal health care is a national problem, not just a state one. The NYHA wouldn’t solve all of our problems, but it would drastically improve – and save – the lives of so many New Yorkers. We have more than enough evidence that health insurance companies are killing and impoverishing us, deliberately. We need to band together and show that we don’t need them anymore. If you’re a union member, please push for your union to support the NYHA if it doesn’t already. Unions resistant to giving up the power of bargaining for health insurance have been one of the biggest blocks to passing it, but taking health insurance off the table will leave more room for unions to bargain for better pay, conditions, and other benefits. And please contact your state senator and assemblymember to let them know that you support the NYHA. May we have a future where no one needs to worry about things like premiums, deductibles, prior authorizations, and plan exceptions.
